transcript:
Meeting header:
16:00 UTC, 2026-06-06 — Duration 48m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (AE - Redwood), Alicia Wong (SE - Redwood), Priya Desai (Solutions Engineer - Redwood, joined 10m in), Samir Rao (CTO - Atlasly), Lena Ortiz (Lead Backend Engineer), Marcus Hill (PM), unknown intern (audio glitch)

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API sandbox live walkthrough. Focus on streaming, parameters, and retry/backoff best practices. Action items captured.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood — appreciate you carving out time. quick round robin?
[00:06] Samir: Samir here, CTO at Atlasly, Lena and Marcus are with me, we'll hand off questions — excited to see streaming stuff.
[00:12] Jordan: awesome — Alicia, you wanna kick the demo?
[00:15] Alicia: sure — hi all, i'm Alicia, i'll run through the hosted chat sandbox and show streaming and example retry flows. i'll flag the common gotchas, and we'll surface console/optimize tips later.
[00:28] Marcus: quick note — we have a real-time chat widget that needs ~low 200ms median latency and cost sensitivity, just FYI.
[00:36] Lena: also security: SSO + audit logs are table stakes for us, we need to see how logs look in the console.
[00:42] Alicia: noted. we'll show the console traces and how token-level cost shows up.

[00:50] Alicia: okay, jumping into the sandbox — i'm using the hosted API key and a small conversation sample. first piece: streaming. you'll see partial tokens arrive as chunked events, we expose an event stream with incremental deltas.
[01:05] [screen share sound — typing]
[01:10] Alicia: here's a simple chat request body: model, messages, temperature, max_tokens, and stream: true. when stream=true the client gets chunks as the model generates. important: partial text can be non-final, so only rely on final flag for completion.
[01:30] Lena: what's the default chunk size? do we control latency by chunk size?
[01:34] Alicia: great question — chunk size is model-internal; we surface partial tokens roughly every 100-300ms depending on model and sequence length. you can tune perceived latency by reducing tokenization overhead (shorter prompts), but chunk cadence is not a param you set.
[01:52] Samir: ok, but what about buffering on our side — we do websockets to browser clients. any best practices?
[01:58] Alicia: yes, use server-side stream forwarder — keep a small buffer, flush on newline or sentence in the UI to avoid jitter. also add a small debounce so UI doesn't re-render every partial token 
[02:12] Jordan: and instrument latency in the console — we show per-request timing so you can see where the delay is (model compute vs network).

[02:20] [crosstalk — inaudible]

[02:30] Alicia: moving to retry behavior: hosted API returns transient 5xx or rate-limit errors. pattern we suggest is idempotency + exponential backoff with jitter. we recommend an idempotency key on generation requests when you might retry.
[02:48] Marcus: we worry about duplicates — if someone gets partial tokens then we retry, client may see duplicated responses. how do we prevent that?
[02:55] Alicia: two techniques: 1) use an idempotency-key so server dedups; 2) design client to stitch partial streams carefully — only accept subsequent content when final event hasn't been received within a short timeout. we commonly pair idempotency with client-side sequence checks.
[03:18] Priya: also mention rehydrating KV cache — if you're using conversation cache, retries should preserve the same cache key so the model's context doesn't drift. some folks call it K-V cash or K-V cache in conversation, there's often transcription slips.
[03:32] Samir: haha yeah K-V cash, noted.

[03:40] Alicia: demo time — i'll trigger a streaming request. look at the response events: data: {delta: 'Hello', index: 0, finish_reason: null} then later finish_reason: 'stop' when done. the client should treat finish_reason as authoritative.
[04:05] [live stream — partial tokens appear on screen]
[04:14] Lena: looks snappy. what's the typical latency for a 128-token response on our size model?
[04:20] Alicia: for a mid-size open model we surface medians in the console — for small sequences you'll often see 80-180ms per chunk, end-to-end 300-800ms depending on model and hardware. we'll run Atlasly's prompts later to be exact.

[04:36] Jordan: quick aside: Optimize recommendations can suggest batching or quant profiles if you need cost reductions. we'll show a sample later.

[04:45] Marcus: can you walk through params — like temp vs top_p? we mix both currently and unsure which to tune.
[04:52] Alicia: temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling — they overlap. typically pick one: temp for coarse control, top_p if you want distribution truncation. for determinism set temp=0 and consider top_p=1. max_tokens caps output length; set stop sequences to avoid run-on responses for chat.

[05:20] Alicia: also show prompt length effects — tokens in prompt count toward context window; trimming earlier messages or storing embeddings for retrieval can reduce token cost.
[05:32] Samir: we use retrieval-augmented generation — will prefix caching help?
[05:36] Alicia: yes — Redwood has prefix/KV caching for repeated context. if you pre-cache stable retrieved text you can avoid re-sending large prefixes and reduce latency and cost. Optimize will flag high-reuse prompts and recommend caching.

[05:52] [pause for screen load]

[06:00] Alicia: now retry patterns, practical pseudocode: try request with idempotency key, on 429 or 5xx do exponential backoff (base 200ms, multiply by 2, jitter), cap at 10s, after N retries fall back to smaller model variant or queue request for later. Avoid blind retries on client for streaming mid-flight — use status and deduping.
[06:26] Marcus: what's N? 3? 4?
[06:29] Alicia: we commonly do 3-4 tries. 3 is a good default for interactive UX.

[06:35] Jordan: i'll call out a common pitfall: retrying on 4xx is wrong — if it's a prompt error or quota error that's not transient. Only 429 or 5xx.

[06:45] [screen shows console trace — timeline view]

[06:50] Alicia: this trace shows per-token timing; in this req you can see a spike at 1.2s because of a large initial KV fetch. the console surfaces that so you can tune caching.
[07:05] Lena: can we export logs for our SIEM? we need full audit trails.
[07:09] Alicia: yes, VPC/private customers can ship audit logs to S3 or forward to your SIEM; hosted exposes structured audit events (user, request id, model, token counts). we'll include security docs in the follow-up.

[07:25] Samir: and encryption at rest? KMS?
[07:28] Jordan: supported — KMS integrations, and we can talk through key management in Private dedicated deployments. for hosted we have tenant encryption and optional BYOK discussions for enterprise.

[07:40] Marcus: back to streaming — do we need websockets? server-sent events?
[07:44] Alicia: we support chunked HTTP streams and websockets; browsers usually use EventSource or websocket proxies. choose based on client needs. our SDKs abstract that away.

[07:56] [10m in, Priya joins — audio beep]
[08:02] Priya: sorry late — joined. picking up — Alicia, could you show an example where a retry leads to duplicate final messages and how idempotency avoids it?
[08:12] Alicia: sure. i'm going to replay a synthetic failure: first request returns 502 after partial stream, client retries with same idempotency key. backend detects same key, returns cached final response rather than starting a new generation. watch request IDs.
[08:28] [demo — logs show request id and idempotency key hit]
[08:36] Priya: nice — that clears dup issue.

[08:40] Lena: for the idempotency store, is there any window/TTL? we worry about storage growth.
[08:46] Alicia: good point — we keep idempotency metadata for a configurable window, default 7 days for hosted, customers can request shorter windows. it stores hash + final response pointer, not entire outputs to reduce storage.

[09:00] Jordan: let's pivot to a quick live throughput note — if you expect spikes, Redwood Dedicated or reserved pools reduce queuing. Hosted has burst capacity but for steady high QPS dedicated is recommended.

[09:18] Samir: our QPS is spiky — baseline 5 rps, peaks 80 rps for short bursts during product launches.
[09:24] Alicia: we typically recommend a hybrid: hosted + burst reservations or dedicated pools during launch windows. Optimize also suggests autoscaling related policies.

[09:36] Marcus: what's the cost implication of streaming? are partial tokens billed?
[09:40] Alicia: we bill on generated + input tokens at token granularity — streaming doesn't change billing model. however perceived cost can change with prompt/length. Optimize will show per-token cost and suggest quantization or smaller model variants for cheap ops.

[09:56] [screen: Optimize console suggestions — batching, quantization profiles]

[10:02] Alicia: here's an Optimize suggestion: for chat short responses we can enable micro-batching (up to 8 concurrent messages) which increases throughput and lowers per-token cost at slight latency tradeoff. there's also a recommended quant profile for your model family which typically saves 30% token CPU.
[10:20] Lena: curious about quality regressions with quantization? we've seen hallucinations increase when overly quantized.
[10:26] Alicia: yes — Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets. it flags regressions against baselines — you can set a threshold for rollback automatic fallback to full-precision model.

[10:40] Marcus: can you show how we set up alerts for quality drift?
[10:44] Alicia: in console we create an eval suite with representative prompts and expected outputs, then set thresholds. when metric delta crosses threshold it sends alerts and can trigger rollbacks. we'll send a screenshot in the follow-up.

[10:56] Samir: great — how long to get a sandbox running with our sample prompts?
[11:00] Jordan: typical: we can spin a sandbox in under an hour if you share a small prompt set and API access. POC with dedicated tests ~1-2 weeks depending on infra.

[11:11] Lena: we need to validate latency under real browser conditions — can you run a small synthetic test?
[11:15] Alicia: yes we'll run Atlasly's prompts — please drop them in the shared doc (we'll paste link).

[11:22] [shared link posted in chat] https://redwood.example.com/sandbox/atlasly

[11:28] Marcus: quick procurement question — do we sign an NDA or do we need a corporate PO to start a sandbox?
[11:33] Jordan: NDA isn't required for a sandbox, but for enterprise integrations we do a DPA and security questionnaires. PO only for dedicated/reserved capacity.

[11:42] Samir: good. also bumping up security review later this month — can you send SOC2 doc?
[11:46] Jordan: yes, will attach SOC2 + security whitepaper in follow-up.

[11:52] Alicia: back to retry playbook — show pseudocode for client.
[11:56] Alicia: 1) attach idempotency key 2) attempt request 3) on 429/5xx -> backoff with jitter (200ms base, max 10s), limit to 3 retries 4) on success validate finish flag 5) log to console for traceability.
[12:14] Marcus: are there SDK helpers for that? we don't want to reimplement.
[12:18] Alicia: yes, Redwood SDK provides retry wrapper with idempotency support and telemetry hooks. we'll point to the JS and Python sample in the repo.

[12:28] Priya: another edge case: what about partial streaming where client disconnects mid-generation — do we continue generating?
[12:36] Alicia: by default the server will try to complete generation unless canceled, but you can send a cancel with request id. for cost-sensitive flows you can configure generator to respect client disconnects immediately.

[12:48] Jordan: let's surface typical error codes and what they mean for UX.
[12:52] Alicia: 401 = auth, don't retry; 403 = forbidden; 429 = rate limit -> retry with backoff; 5xx -> transient -> retry; 413 = payload too large -> truncate prompt, don't retry.

[13:08] Lena: we use a middleware for prompt trimming to keep tokens low. any tooling to measure token usage per route?
[13:14] Alicia: console shows token counts per request per route and per API key — it's searchable. you can set alerts when token cost per minute climbs.

[13:28] Marcus: can we do A/B model rollouts? we'd like 10% traffic to smaller cheaper model.
[13:34] Alicia: yes, rollouts are first-class: canary rules, percentage traffic, model pinned per route, automatic fallback to older version if error spike. we'll demo the rollout UI in the console during a later session.

[13:50] [screen show quick route config mock]

[14:00] Samir: final question: for initial POC, recommend hosted or dedicated?
[14:04] Alicia: start hosted for speed; if steady high QPS or strict data residency then move to Dedicated or Private. Hosted supports private networking via VPC peering in many regions.

[14:15] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps.
[14:18] Jordan: Jordan will send pricing and SOC2/security docs; Alicia will run latency tests against Atlasly prompts and share results; Lena will provide prompt samples and expected traffic shape; schedule POC kickoff.
[14:28] Samir: sounds good. Marcus, Lena — any final concerns?
[14:32] Marcus: no more from me, thanks.
[14:34] Lena: all good — thanks, excited to try the sandbox.
[14:38] [meeting end wrap-up, small chitchat]

--- End transcript ---
